items.prompt: Marula Foods dries fruit in Gobabis for sale across Namibia. Define supply.
items.canonical_answer: Supply is the quantity of a good that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a period of time. For Marula Foods, supply is the quantity of dried fruit it is willing and able to offer for sale at each price over a period - not the quantity it hopes buyers might take.
marking_guidance: One mark for the precise definition: willing and able, at a given price, over a period of time - the meaning must place supply on the seller's side of the market.
One mark for applying the meaning to Marula Foods: what it offers for sale at each price, rather than what it hopes to sell.

items.prompt: Otjiwa Dairy in Otavi offers 500 litres of milk a week at N$10 a litre. The farm-gate price rises to N$12 a litre, and the dairy offers 620 litres a week. Discuss how a supply diagram of this market shows what supply means, giving a verbal walk-through of every part of the diagram and what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Walk through the diagram in words, element by element. First, the axes labelled: price of milk, in N$ per litre, on the vertical axis, and quantity, in litres a week, on the horizontal axis. Second, the original curves drawn and labelled: an upward-sloping supply curve S through the point at N$10 and 500 litres, showing the quantity the dairy is willing and able to offer at each price; the market's demand curve may be drawn in faintly, since it belongs to topic 2.3, to mark where the two sides meet. Third, the shift or movement, in the correct direction: the price rise is a movement up along the unchanged supply curve - an extension in supply - from the point at N$10 and 500 litres to the point at N$12 and 620 litres, because the good's own price is what changed. Fourth, the new equilibrium marked and labelled: the point at N$12 and 620 litres, where the quantity the dairy now offers meets what buyers take at the new price. Fifth, what the diagram shows, in words: at each point along S the dairy shows effective supply - willingness and ability to offer for sale - at that price, so the curve is the definition of supply drawn as a relationship. The link is that the diagram joins the definition to the selling side of the market, and the consequence is that 120 more litres a week are offered, since 620 - 500 = 120 litres, because the higher price makes each litre more worth producing.
marking_guidance: The walk-through must name the axes labelled - price and quantity, each with its units - before anything else.
Reward the original curves drawn and labelled: the supply curve in place at N$10 and 500 litres before the change is described.
Check the shift or movement, in the correct direction: a rise in the good's own price is a movement up an unchanged supply curve, an extension in supply, not a shift of it.
The new equilibrium marked and labelled at the new price and quantity earns its mark, and what the diagram shows, in words, must close the walk-through.
The link between the definition and its drawn form, and the consequence for the market - 120 more litres a week offered - carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: Namib Signs paints standard signs for Windhoek shops. Its schedule: at N$100 a sign it offers 24 signs a month, at N$150 it offers 40 signs, at N$200 it offers 52 signs. Explain what the figures show about Namib Signs' supply of signs.
items.canonical_answer: What the data shows is the definition of supply written as numbers: at each price, the quantity of signs the firm is willing and able to offer. The relationship is positive - the higher the price, the larger the quantity offered. Supporting evidence: at N$100 the firm offers 24 signs a month and at N$200 it offers 52, since 52 - 24 = 28 more signs, because a higher price makes each sign more worth painting and so raises the quantity the firm is willing to offer. However, the comparison of the steps suggests ability has a limit: the offering rises by 16 signs between N$100 and N$150, since 40 - 24 = 16 signs, but by 12 signs between N$150 and N$200, since 52 - 40 = 12 signs, so the firm may be nearing what its painters and machines are able to produce in a month.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - a positive relationship between price and quantity offered - must be named before the evidence is credited.
Supporting evidence: the comparison of 24 signs at N$100 with 52 at N$200, both figures read from the schedule.
An exception or reservation - the shrinking steps - earns its mark where the explanation of the relationship is sound.
The why must be given: a higher price makes production more worthwhile, which is the explanation of the relationship.

items.prompt: Kaoko Juice would like to sell 1 000 bottles of juice a week in Opuwo, but its pressing plant is able to produce 400 bottles a week. Explain whether Kaoko Juice's wish to sell 1 000 bottles is supply at present.
items.canonical_answer: The figures mean that Kaoko Juice's supply at present is the 400 bottles a week it is both willing and able to offer, because supply needs willingness and ability together: a wish to sell 1 000 bottles without the capacity to press them stays outside supply, and the gap is 600 bottles a week, since 1 000 - 400 = 600 bottles. Therefore the wish is not supply at present; it becomes supply provided the firm raises its pressing capacity, assuming the extra bottles could be produced and sold at the going price.
marking_guidance: The context must be used: the figures are a wish of 1 000 bottles against a capacity of 400.
The reasoning is that supply is willingness and ability together, because a wish without the ability to offer stays outside supply.
The conclusion must state what the figures mean: the firm's supply at present is 400 bottles a week, not 1 000, unless capacity grows.

items.prompt: Etosha Gate Lodge near Etosha charges N$650 a night and lets 34 of its 40 rooms to visitors. The nightly rate rises to N$800, and the lodge now lets 40 rooms - each room it has. Analyse the effect of this price rise on the quantity of rooms the lodge offers, on the lodge itself and on visitors.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: the initial change is the lodge's own price, rising from N$650 to N$800 a night. Mechanism: because each room brings in more per night, letting rooms becomes more worthwhile, and this causes an extension in supply - a movement up along the lodge's unchanged supply curve - from 34 rooms toward the 40 it has standing; the lodge is willing to let more rooms at N$800 and able to, since the rooms exist. Consequence: therefore the quantity of rooms offered rises from 34 to 40, since 40 - 34 = 6 rooms, and the lodge has reached the limit of what it is able to offer - beyond 40 rooms a willingness to let more counts for nothing without the ability, which is what the definition of supply turns on. For whom: for the lodge, 6 more room-nights sold at the higher rate; for visitors, 6 more rooms to book, at N$800 rather than N$650 a night; for the lodge's cleaners and guides, more rooms let may mean longer shifts.
marking_guidance: The chain needs its starting point: the good's own price rising, with the quantity moving along an unchanged curve.
The mechanism mark rewards the because-step: a higher price makes letting rooms more worthwhile, and this causes the extension along the curve.
The consequence must be worked through: therefore the quantity offered rises to the lodge's limit of 40 rooms, 6 more than before.
For whom: consequences must be named for the lodge, for visitors and for the lodge's workers.

items.prompt: Ruacana Riverside Cabins runs guided canoe trips on the Kunene, offering 12 trips a week at N$150 a trip. Explain what the definition of supply includes, using the case of the cabins' trips.
items.canonical_answer: The definition includes five features. A quantity offered for sale: the trips themselves, counted as 12 a week. Willingness to sell: the firm is willing to run trips at N$150 because each trip is worth running at that price. Ability to offer: it has the canoes, the guides and the river access to run the trips - without them the willingness would count for nothing. A given price: N$150 a trip, the price at which the 12 trips are offered. A period of time: a week, over which the quantity is counted. The features together are what makes the 12 trips supply rather than a hope to sell trips.
marking_guidance: The features must be drawn from the definition: a quantity, willingness, ability, a given price, a period of time.
Each feature is explained through the case: the 12 trips, the N$150 price, the canoes and guides, the week.
The characteristics are complete when willingness and ability are both shown - what it includes is both halves of the definition.

items.prompt: Oshakati Textiles sells printed cloth from its depot at N$25 a metre. Define quantity supplied.

One mark for the contrast that fixes the definition: quantity supplied is a single point on the supply curve, whereas supply is the whole relationship.

items.prompt: A Walvis Bay fishing firm's schedule for horse mackerel: at N$15 a kilogram it offers 800 kilograms a day, at N$20 it offers 950 kilograms, at N$25 it offers 1 050 kilograms. Explain what the figures show about the firm's supply of mackerel as the price changes.

items.prompt: The price of a 10-kilogram crate of tomatoes at the Oshakati fresh-produce market falls from N$60 to N$45. Analyse the effect of the price fall on the quantity of tomatoes traders offer for sale, on the traders and on shoppers.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: the initial change is the crate's own price, falling from N$60 to N$45. Mechanism: because each crate earns less, hauling and sorting it is less worth the traders' effort, and this causes a contraction in supply - a movement down along the unchanged supply curve - as some crates are no longer worth bringing to market at N$45. Consequence: therefore the quantity of tomatoes offered for sale tends to fall, and the market settles at a smaller quantity than before, without the supply curve itself moving. For whom: for the traders, fewer crates to sell means thinner takings per stall; for the traders' porters, fewer crates to haul may mean shorter working days; for shoppers, fewer crates on the benches at each price, though at N$45 instead of N$60 for those that are there.
marking_guidance: The chain needs its starting point: the good's own price falling, with the quantity moving along an unchanged curve.
The mechanism mark rewards the because-step: a lower price makes each crate less worth hauling, and this causes the contraction along the curve.
The consequence must be worked through: therefore the quantity offered tends to fall, and the results are stated without shifting the curve.
For whom: consequences must be named for the traders, for their workers and for shoppers.

items.prompt: Explain the features of an extension in supply and of a contraction in supply.
items.canonical_answer: An extension in supply has three features: it is caused by a rise in the good's own price; it is a movement up along an unchanged supply curve; and it ends at a larger quantity offered than before. A contraction in supply has the matching three: it is caused by a fall in the good's own price; it is a movement down along the same unchanged curve; and it ends at a smaller quantity offered. The feature the two share is that the supply curve itself stays where it was - what changes is the quantity supplied, a point on the curve, and the element that keeps them movements rather than shifts is that the good's own price is the sole influence at work.
marking_guidance: The features of an extension are named: a price rise, a movement up along the curve, a larger quantity offered.
The features of a contraction mirror them: a price fall, a movement down, a smaller quantity offered.
The characteristic that carries the mark is that the curve does not shift - what it includes is a change in quantity supplied, not a change in supply.

items.prompt: Bread in Katutura comes from many small bakeries. Define market supply.
items.canonical_answer: Market supply is the quantity of a good that all the producers in a market together are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a period of time. For bread in Katutura, it is the loaves the town's bakeries together offer, not the output of a single bakery.
marking_guidance: One mark for the precise definition: all the producers together, willing and able, at a given price, over a period of time.
One mark for the meaning of "market" here: the combined offering of every seller, against the individual supply of one bakery.

items.prompt: Katutura's bread at N$8 a loaf comes from three bakeries: One Bread offers 200 loaves a day, Tuwani Bakery offers 300, and Eveline Street Bakers offers 500. Explain why market supply at N$8 a loaf is found by adding the bakeries' offerings together rather than by taking the largest or an average.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that market supply counts what every seller in the market offers at that price, so the market figure at N$8 is the sum of the individual figures at N$8. Adding across bakeries: 200 + 300 = 500 loaves, and 500 + 500 = 1 000 loaves a day. Taking the largest bakery's output alone would leave the other two bakeries' offerings out and understate the market; an average would divide what three bakeries offer between them, as if one bakery stood in for the whole market. Because supply at a price is what all the sellers together offer, the purpose of adding across sellers at the same price is to count the whole market.
marking_guidance: The reason must be stated: market supply at one price is the sum of what every seller offers at that price, which is the purpose of the method.
Reward the working across sellers at the same price: 200 + 300 = 500 loaves, then 500 + 500 = 1 000 loaves a day.
The largest or the average misreads the method because each drops sellers from the count or divides the market's offering between them.

The conclusion is that the market supply of flowers at N$30 is 1 000 bunches a week, built from the farm's 300, the grower's 450 and the rest of the market's 250 - and the same addition done at each other price fills in the whole market supply schedule.

The reasoning is that market supply at one price is the sum of every seller's offering at that price, because the market counts them all.
The conclusion must state the total with its unit: 1 000 bunches a week at N$30 a bunch.

items.prompt: Marula Foods of Gobabis dries fruit for sale across Namibia. Its offering at an unchanged price of N$40 a packet: 900 packets in March, 900 in April, 750 in May, 600 in June. In May the cost of its packaging rose; in June the marula harvest came in smaller. Explain what the figures show about the supply of dried fruit at Marula Foods.
items.canonical_answer: What the data shows is a decrease in supply: at an unchanged price the quantity offered fell in May and again in June, so the whole supply curve shifted left rather than the market moving along it. Supporting evidence: 900 packets in March and April, then 750 in May and 600 in June - 300 fewer by June, since 900 - 600 = 300 packets - at the same N$40. The explanation of the relationship is that a packaging cost rise is a condition of supply, making each packet less worth producing, and a smaller harvest cuts the firm's ability to offer fruit at any price. However, the figures show the two conditions arriving together: they cannot separate how much of the 300-packet fall came from the dearer packaging and how much from the smaller harvest, and a fall in buyers' demand over the same months could have thinned sales as well.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - a decrease in supply at an unchanged price, a shift of the curve - must be named first.
Supporting evidence: the comparison of 900 packets with 750 and 600 at the same N$40, all read from the figures.
The exception or reservation - the two conditions cannot be separated, and demand may have moved too - earns its mark.
The why must be given: a cost rise and a smaller harvest are conditions of supply, which is the explanation of the relationship.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Which best defines supply?
A  the amount sellers hope buyers might take, whether or not they can produce it
B  the quantity producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a period of time
C  the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at each price
D  the amount sold at any price over any length of time

2. A fishing firm in Walvis Bay would like to sell 2 000 kilograms of hake a week, but its boats are able to land 1 200 kilograms. The firm's supply of hake a week at present:
A  is 2 000 kilograms, because willingness is what counts
B  is 1 200 kilograms, because the ability to offer stops at what the boats can land
C  is 3 200 kilograms, adding the wish to the catch
D  cannot be known from the figures

3. As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied tends to:
A  rise, because producing the good becomes more worthwhile
B  fall, because dearer goods put sellers off
C  stay the same, because supply is a fixed number
D  shift the supply curve to the right

4. The price of a good rises. On a supply diagram this shows:
A  a shift of the whole supply curve to the right
B  a movement up along the supply curve
C  a shift of the whole supply curve to the left
D  no change of any kind

5. Market supply at N$25 a metre is found by:
A  adding every producer's quantity offered at N$25
B  adding one producer's quantities across all the prices
C  taking the largest producer's output as the market total
D  averaging the producers' outputs at N$25

6. A fall in the costs of the inputs used to make a good tends to:
A  shift the supply curve to the left
B  shift the supply curve to the right
C  move the market down along the supply curve
D  leave supply where it was, because costs are not prices

7. Which is a condition of supply?
A  the good's own price
B  the number of sellers in the market
C  the income of the good's buyers
D  the quantity sold last month

8. A subsidy of N$5 a metre is paid to cloth producers, and the price of cloth stays at N$25 a metre. The subsidy tends to:
A  increase supply, shifting the curve to the right
B  decrease supply, shifting the curve to the left
C  cause a contraction in supply along the curve
D  raise quantity supplied by moving the market along the curve
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 B, 3 A, 4 B, 5 A, 6 B, 7 B, 8 A.
1. B is the definition - willing and able, at a price, over time. A counts a wish as supply and misses the ability to offer; C describes demand, the buying side; D drops the given price and the period that pin the quantity down.
2. B: willingness without the ability to offer stays outside supply. A lets the wish stand alone; C invents a total by adding a wish to a catch; D misses that the figures already state what the firm is able to land.
3. A is the positive relationship at work. B inverts the relationship; C treats supply as a fixed number rather than a relationship; D confuses a change in quantity supplied with a shift of the curve.
4. B: the good's own price moves the market along the curve. A and C confuse a movement with a shift, which is caused by a condition of supply; D denies the change the question states.
5. A adds across producers at one price, which is what market supply means. B adds across prices for one producer, a different question; C drops the smaller producers; D divides the market's offering instead of counting it.
6. B: cheaper inputs make production more worthwhile at each price, so the curve shifts right. A reverses the direction; C mistakes a cost change for the good's own price falling; D misses that costs are a condition of supply.
7. B: the number of sellers is an influence other than the good's own price, so it shifts the curve. A is the price that moves the market along the curve; C belongs to the demand side; D is an outcome of the market, not an influence on supply.
8. A: a subsidy is a condition of supply, so with the price unchanged the whole curve shifts right. B reverses the direction; C names a movement along the curve that a price change would cause; D mistakes a shift for a movement.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option for each is listed and every distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Each distractor traces to a named error: a wish counted as supply, demand confused with supply, a movement confused with a shift, addition across prices confused with addition across producers, and an outcome confused with a condition.

items.prompt:
A radio report from Oshakati, October 2026: "Tomatoes are the Oshakati fresh-produce market's steadiest trade. Traders offered 1 100 crates a week last year at N$85 a crate; this year they offer 1 400 crates a week at the same N$85. Two things changed: good rains lifted the harvest round Ruacana, and a new feeder road cut the cost of bringing each crate to market. A fuel levy of N$6 on every crate arrives next year."

Table 1 - Oshakati tomatoes
  crates offered a week: 1 100 last year, 1 400 this year
  price a crate: N$85 last year, N$85 this year
  rain round Ruacana: poor last year, good this year
  road cost a crate: high last year, lower this year
  fuel levy a crate: none this year, N$6 next year

(a) Calculate the rise in the number of crates offered a week. [1]
(b) Identify from Table 1 one condition of supply that changed between the two years. [2]
(c) Explain why the quantity of tomatoes offered rose even though the price did not change. [4]
(d) Analyse what the figures suggest about the tomato market next year, for the traders, their customers and the truck owners. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 1 400 - 1 100 = 300 crates.
(b) Either the better rain round Ruacana (the weather) or the cheaper road cost a crate (a fall in the costs of getting the good to market). Each is a condition of supply: an influence other than the crate's own price.
(c) An unchanged price with a larger quantity offered cannot come from a movement along an unchanged supply curve, because along the curve a higher price is what raises quantity supplied. What fits the figures is an increase in supply: conditions changed - the harvest was bigger and transport cheaper - so at the unchanged price of N$85 the whole curve shifted right and 300 more crates were offered. The quantity rose because the whole relationship moved, not because the price did.
(d) Expected relationship: the fuel levy raises the cost of bringing each crate to market, so supply tends to shift left next year. Evidence: the levy is N$6 a crate, against this year's 1 400 crates offered at N$85 with the good rains and the cheaper road behind them. Analysis: for the traders, dearer transport means some crates are no longer worth hauling, so the quantity offered at N$85 tends to fall back from 1 400; for customers, fewer crates at each price may mean emptier benches, and where traders pass the levy on, dearer tomatoes; for the truck owners, the levy may lift what they can charge for haulage, since hauling costs more to run. Exception: however, if the rains stay good, the larger harvest may offset the levy and keep the quantity offered near this year's level.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are read from the data; the six-mark part must use the figures as evidence - the 300-crate rise, the N$85 price held flat, the N$6 levy - and one point is marked per distinct linked statement.
Part (c) is marked on the shift of the curve against the movement along it; the distinction, and the link from the changed conditions to the extra 300 crates, carries the marks.

Part (d) is marked on expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception; quoting figures without the relationship they support earns nothing, and consequences must be named for the traders, the customers and the truck owners.

facts: crates offered last year 1 100 a week
price a crate N$85 both years
crates offered this year 1 400 a week
fuel levy N$6 a crate next year
good rains round Ruacana this year
new feeder road cut transport cost

items.prompt:
Oshakati Textiles weaves cloth sold across northern Namibia. Answer all parts.

(a) Define supply. [2]
(b) Explain the difference between supply and quantity supplied. [4]
(c) The government pays Oshakati Textiles a subsidy of N$5 a metre while the price of cloth stays at N$25 a metre, and the firm's offering rises from 5 000 to 5 600 metres a month. Analyse what this change means for the firm, for its workers and for its customers. [6]
(d) Discuss whether a rise in the price of cloth would increase the supply of cloth. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Supply is the quantity of a good that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a period of time.
(b) Supply is the whole relationship between price and quantity: the full set of quantities producers offer at each price. Quantity supplied is the single amount offered at one particular price. When the good's own price changes, quantity supplied changes and the market moves along the supply curve, while supply - the relationship - stays as it was. When a condition of supply changes, the whole curve shifts, and quantity supplied changes at an unchanged price. The test is whether the good's own price changed.
(c) Starting point: the initial change is a condition of supply - the N$5 a metre subsidy - with the price fixed at N$25. Mechanism: because a condition changed while the price did not, the supply curve shifts to the right, and this causes the quantity supplied at N$25 to rise from 5 000 to 5 600 metres a month, an increase of 600 metres, since 5 600 - 5 000 = 600 metres. Consequence for the firm: more metres sold at an unchanged price, with each metre carrying the subsidy alongside the N$25. Consequence for its workers: more metres to weave may mean more shifts or extra hands taken on. Consequence for customers: more cloth on the market at N$25, and if other weavers gain the same subsidy, the market price may ease later. Exception: if the subsidy is withdrawn, the curve shifts back and the extra metres disappear.
(d) The case for: the relationship between price and quantity supplied is positive, so a higher price tends to raise the quantity supplied - a movement up along an unchanged supply curve - as each metre becomes more worth weaving, and sellers offer more cloth. The case against: a price rise changes quantity supplied, not supply; the curve itself has not moved, so calling the change an increase in supply mistakes a movement along the curve for a shift of it. Where input costs rise alongside the price, the curve may even shift left while the market slides up it, and the quantity offered could end up smaller. Judgement: a higher price raises the quantity supplied provided the supply curve itself is not shifting at the same time; whether supply increases depends on a condition of supply changing, and that is the condition the judgement rests on.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise definition: willing and able, at a given price, over a period of time.
(b) one mark per distinct point: the whole relationship against the single amount at one price, a movement along against a shift, each with the link made.

(c) one mark per distinct linked statement from the starting point - the subsidy at an unchanged price - through the mechanism, a shift of the curve, to the consequence for the firm, its workers and its customers.

(d) Level 3 examines why it might - the positive relationship - and why it might not - the curve itself has not shifted - and reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side; Level 1 asserts.

facts: price of cloth fixed at N$25 a metre
offering rose from 5 000 to 5 600 metres a month

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "The cost of the vinyl that sign-painting firms print on falls sharply. Discuss whether firms like Namib Signs in Windhoek are likely to sell more signs next year without changing their prices." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for: an input cost is a condition of supply, so the fall tends to shift the supply curve to the right; at an unchanged price, the quantity offered rises, and the firm may sell more without touching its price.
Chain 1: vinyl cost falls -> each sign is cheaper to produce -> the supply curve shifts right -> at the fixed price, the quantity offered rises -> sales rise (for the firm, for its customers).
Case against, first point: the demand for signs may move against the firm - if Windhoek shops cut their spending on signage next year, the extra offered meets weaker buying, and sales fail to rise even with more supplied.
Chain 2: shops spend less on signage -> at each price fewer signs are bought -> the larger offering meets weaker demand -> sales stay flat or fall (for the firm).
Case against, second point: other conditions of supply may offset the vinyl saving - a rise in wage costs or a levy on paints could shift the curve back towards its old place.
Chain 3: wage costs rise -> the vinyl saving is offset -> the curve shifts back towards S1 -> the offering at the unchanged price barely grows (for the firm, its customers).
Judgement: the firm should expect to sell more provided the cost fall is not offset by other conditions and the demand for signs does not move against it. The condition the judgement depends on: what happens to the other conditions of supply - wages, taxes, the number of rival sign-painters - and to the demand for signs over the year.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the stated judgement is what is assessed.
The plan must carry the case for and the case against, each developed as a chain from condition to consequence, and name the parties - the firm, its customers.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: the behaviour of the other conditions of supply and of the demand for signs.
What settles it: whether the firm's own supply curve stays shifted right once the rest of the year's changes are counted - the decisive test is which way its own curve sits by year's end.
